sections.heading: How much does freelance software development cost?
sections.text:
There is no reliable single price for every app, website or SaaS product. A quote depends on what users must do, how many roles need access, the integrations involved, existing content or data, and the work needed to test and launch it. Gagan Shukla provides a project-specific written quote after reviewing your requirements; this guide does not publish a starting price or imply that every project fits one package.

For a useful comparison, send the same brief to each developer. A cheaper total may exclude design, backend work, deployment, testing or handover that another quote includes. Ask each supplier to list assumptions, exclusions and recurring costs.

sections.heading: Website, mobile app and SaaS scopes differ
sections.text:
A business website: content, service pages, contact forms, editing needs, mobile layout and the launch setup.
A mobile app: Android or iOS targets, user journeys, backend, authentication, permissions, notifications, offline behaviour and store submission.
A SaaS product: tenant access, customer onboarding, subscription rules, admin tools, support workflows and hosting.
A CRM or HRMS: staff roles, approval rules, records, reports and migration from existing systems.
A logistics product: dispatcher and driver workflows, trip states, location requirements, proof of delivery and network failure handling.

Choose one essential end-to-end workflow for the first release. List later features separately so a version-one quote does not silently include your entire long-term roadmap.

sections.heading: Separate development fees from running costs
sections.text:
Your development contract and your software operating costs are separate decisions. Hosting, domains, SMS, maps, payment-provider charges, email services and app-store accounts may have recurring or usage-based fees. Your business should own the relevant accounts and review the providers’ current charges before approval.

Ask which third-party accounts you need and who will pay their invoices.
Specify whether data migration, content writing and translation are included.
Record which launch tasks and handover documents are included.
Agree the support period and how later feature requests are priced.

sections.heading: What determines the delivery timeline?
sections.text:
A credible timeline follows the agreed scope. It also depends on the availability of content, design approvals, integration documentation, test accounts and the person accepting each milestone. Store reviews and third-party approvals are external dependencies and should not be promised as fixed dates controlled by the developer.

Break delivery into reviewable milestones: discovery and scope, approved workflows, a working core journey, integration and testing, then launch and handover. Each milestone needs an acceptance checklist, not only a calendar date.

sections.heading: Compare a fixed quote and a freelance retainer
sections.text: A fixed-scope quote suits a clearly defined website, app release or MVP. A freelance retainer suits ongoing changes when priorities evolve and you want an agreed block of development time. In both cases, document deliverables, review hours, ownership and a process for approving additional work. These are freelance contracts, not employment offers.

sections.heading: Finding the best web developer for a website or web app
sections.text:
For a marketing website, examine whether visitors can understand the offer and enquire easily on a phone. A polished homepage and a reliable internal application require different checks.

Check useful content, navigation, mobile layout and keyboard access.
Discuss page rendering, canonical URLs and content editing where relevant.
Test contact forms, error states and the handover process.
Ask how hosting, domain access and recurring costs will be managed.
Agree on how changes are reviewed before production release.

Milestones you can review through demonstrations.

sections.heading: Start with one operational workflow
sections.text:
A logistics application can mean a driver app, truck booking platform, operations dashboard, fleet system or field-agent CRM. Those products share some building blocks, but they solve different problems. Describe one workflow from start to finish: who creates the job, who accepts it, who changes its status and who needs to see the result.

I have worked on TruckMitr and TMConnect and offer freelance logistics development for Indian and international businesses. This checklist covers decisions to make for a new project; it does not claim that every feature below was included in those earlier applications.

sections.heading: Define drivers, vehicles, jobs and permissions
sections.text:
Who can register a driver or vehicle, and who reviews the record?
Who creates, assigns, accepts, cancels or closes a job?
Which information belongs to a driver, agent, customer or operations manager?
Which changes need a review step or activity history?
Do different branches or business customers need separate views?

Write down the allowed status changes and the person responsible for each one. This helps prevent a driver app and an office dashboard from showing inconsistent operational states. It also makes testing concrete: each role should see and change only what the workflow permits.

sections.heading: Plan explicitly for weak networks
sections.text:
Decide which information a driver needs while offline, which actions can be queued and which actions require an immediate server response. A stored form and live vehicle location behave differently when connectivity disappears. The screen should make pending synchronisation visible rather than reporting success too early.

Define the records available offline and their retention period.
Agree on retry rules and protection against duplicate submissions.
Decide what happens if two people update the same job.
Provide clear pending, failed and completed states.
Test interrupted requests and app restarts during synchronisation.

sections.heading: Scope location tracking and alerts
sections.text:
Describe why location is needed and who should see it. Agree on update frequency, battery expectations, foreground and background behaviour, and what the dashboard shows when location is stale. Location permissions and device limitations need to be part of the product design.

For notifications, define the event, recipient and useful next action. An assignment alert should lead to the correct job. A missed update should have a clear follow-up path. Choose provider integrations after the notification requirements are understood.

sections.heading: Identify integrations and office reporting
sections.text:
Existing CRM or ERP and the API access it provides.
Maps, messages, payment or accounting providers.
Required job, customer and driver exports.
Reports that operations managers need daily.
Who owns the external accounts and pays recurring charges.

Avoid promising an integration before checking the available documentation, access and business rules. If you have existing data, list what must be migrated and which records must remain accessible. The first phase can focus on the most useful workflow while later integrations remain separately scoped.

sections.heading: Ask for a scope you can test
sections.text:
For a first release, choose one driver or staff workflow, the corresponding office view and a clear definition of completion. Include the roles, error states and offline cases in the acceptance criteria. Review the working product at milestones rather than waiting until the final delivery.

“Yes” to every feature without discussing trade-offs.

intro: Choose Flutter or React Native around your product’s device requirements and the team maintaining it. I have used both frameworks in portfolio projects, including Flutter for TMConnect and React Native for TruckMitr. Compare existing skills, native integrations, offline behaviour and release ownership before treating either framework as the automatic cheaper option.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
Both Flutter and React Native let you launch on Android and iOS from one codebase, which typically saves significant time and cost compared with building two native apps. Both are production-proven. The right choice depends on your product, your existing team and your roadmap, not on which framework is “better”.

I have shipped production apps in both: TruckMitr and an HRMS & CRM app in React Native; AURA, GlowCart, HashKart and TMConnect in Flutter. Here is how I advise clients.

sections.heading: Choose Flutter when…
sections.text:
Your app is design-led, with custom animations, branded UI and pixel-perfect consistency across devices.
You want the same UI on Android, iOS and possibly web or desktop from a single codebase.
You do not already have a React web team that needs to share code with the app.
You need smooth performance on a wide range of budget Android devices.

sections.heading: Choose React Native when…
sections.text:
Your company already has a React / Next.js web app and you want to share logic, types or developers.
The app should feel closest to platform-native controls.
You rely on JavaScript/TypeScript libraries or want to hire from the large JavaScript talent pool.
You want over-the-air updates for quick fixes between store releases.

sections.heading: What matters more than the framework
sections.text:
In my experience, product success depends far more on architecture decisions than on Flutter vs React Native:

Offline-first data handling if users have unreliable networks.
A clean backend and database design that can grow with you.
Analytics and crash reporting from day one.
A release process for both app stores, including review timelines.

If you are unsure, start with the user experience you need and the team you have. A good developer will recommend the framework that fits those, not the one they prefer.

sections.heading: Start with an off-the-shelf CRM, unless one of these is true
sections.text: Zoho, HubSpot and Salesforce are excellent products. For a small team with a standard sales pipeline, they are usually the right first step. A custom CRM starts to make sense when the tool begins to shape your business instead of the other way around.

sections.heading: Signs you have outgrown an off-the-shelf CRM
sections.text:
Per-seat licences are growing faster than revenue as you add telecallers, field agents or franchisees.
Your team keeps a parallel spreadsheet because the CRM cannot model your process (site visits, quotations, service tickets, dealer networks).
Field staff need a simple mobile app that works offline, not a complex desktop dashboard.
You need deep integration with your own systems: ERP, billing, inventory, WhatsApp or a customer app.
Customer data must be hosted in a specific region or stay fully under your control.

sections.heading: What a custom CRM typically includes
sections.text:
Lead capture from website forms, ads and calls, with automatic assignment.
Custom pipeline stages that match your real sales process.
Mobile apps for telecallers and field agents, with call logging and visit check-ins.
Role-based access for admins, managers and agents.
Automated follow-up reminders via push, email or WhatsApp.
Dashboards for conversion, team performance and revenue.

I built exactly this kind of system with TMConnect, a Flutter CRM for telecallers and field agents, and an HRMS & CRM app published on both app stores.

sections.heading: A quick build-vs-buy checklist
sections.text:
Will licence costs over the next 3 years exceed a one-time build plus hosting?
Is your sales process a competitive advantage that generic tools flatten?
Do you have field or mobile-first users?
Do you need to own your data and integrations end to end?

If you answered yes to two or more, a custom CRM, often built in phases starting with the most painful workflow, is worth a written scope review.
